stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the cardiology clinic by his parents for follow-up of tetralogy of Fallot.  The diagnosis was made during routine antenatal sonography, and the pregnancy and delivery were otherwise uncomplicated.  The patient has been seen frequently in the clinic and has had no cyanosis, respiratory distress, or difficulty feeding.  The parents become concerned when their son's surgical plan is discussed because he does not have the clinical signs demonstrated by other children with tetralogy of Fallot.  Which of the following is the greatest determinant of symptom severity in this condition?​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​

options.text: Degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of associated pulmonary parenchymal malformations

explanation:
Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) is a congenital heart defect characterized by right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, a ventricular septal defect (VSD), an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.  Because the VSD is invariably large and unrestrictive, right and left ventricular pressures are generally equal, and the magnitude and direction of shunting through the VSD are determined by the relative resistances of the ventricular outflow tracts (Choice E).  Therefore, the greatest determinant of symptom severity is the degree of RVOT obstruction:

  • Severe RVOT obstruction:  Insufficient pulmonary arterial flow with obligatory right-to-left ventricular shunting leads to hypoxemia and profound cyanosis requiring medical/surgical intervention in the immediate neonatal period.

  • Moderate RVOT obstruction:  Moderate obstruction typically permits adequate pulmonary arterial flow and oxygenation.  These patients are acyanotic at baseline due to left-to-right or neutral shunting through the VSD.  However, some degree of the RVOT obstruction is dynamic, and transient increases in RVOT obstruction (eg, infundibular muscle spasm while feeding or crying) may force the reversal of flow (ie, right-to-left) and cause episodic cyanosis.

  • Mild RVOT obstruction:  Patients with mild RVOT, which is likely the case in this boy, may have no cyanotic episodes and develop heart failure later in childhood due to pulmonary overcirculation from the high volume of left-to-right shunting via the large VSD.

(Choices A and C)  Although the pulmonic valve may be stenotic in patients with ToF (contributing to RVOT obstruction), the aortic and tricuspid valves are typically normal and have no stenosis or insufficiency.

(Choice D)  The majority of patients with ToF do not have pulmonary parenchymal or other extracardiac malformations.

Educational objective:Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect characterized by right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, a large ventricular septal defect (VSD), an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.  The degree of RVOT obstruction is the greatest determinant of symptom severity because it regulates pulmonary arterial blood flow and the magnitude and direction of shunting through the VSD.​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​
